preamble: A palatalized alveolar lateral [lʲ] (or a lateral fused with a following yod, [lj]) becomes a true palatal lateral [ʎ], the tongue body taking over the whole closure. In Romance, Latin [lj] (from l + unstressed i/e in hiatus, as in FĪLIUS, FOLIA) yielded [ʎ] throughout Western Romance and in Central and Southern Italy, preserved as Italian gli, Portuguese lh and Catalan ll; in Castilian the outcome is [ʒ] > [x] (fīlius > fijo > hijo) and in Romanian [j], with [ʎ] reconstructed as the intermediate stage. In Goidelic, word-initial slender l corresponds to palatalized [lʲ] in Irish but to the palatal lateral [ʎ] in Scottish Gaelic.

examples.note: Catalan ll continues the palatal lateral from Latin [lj], merging with the [ʎ] from Latin -ll- and initial l-; most Balearic and some eastern dialects later delateralized it to [j].
In Central and Southern Italy [lj] gave a geminate palatal lateral; compare aglio [ˈaʎʎo] 'garlic' < allium and foglia [ˈfɔʎʎa] 'leaf' < folia.
Portuguese spells the result lh and keeps it as [ʎ]; compare mulher [muˈʎɛɾ] 'woman' < mulierem. Rural Central Brazilian Portuguese later delateralized it to [j] (filho [ˈfij]).

examples.from: Old Irish lebor 'book', with word-initial strong slender (palatalized) lateral
examples.note: Irish has a palatalized alveolar lateral in the same word (Connacht [ˈl̠ʲauəɾˠ], Ulster [l̠ʲoːɾˠ]), while Scottish Gaelic realizes word-initial slender l as the palatal lateral [ʎ] in Lewis, Harris, Uist, Barra and Wester Ross; the Irish–Scottish correspondence points to a Scottish shift of the palatalized lateral to [ʎ].
